unit.title: Perform internal and external customer service

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which of these people is served by the welders but works for the same shop?
options: A hotel that orders a steel stairway
A walk-in client who wants a gate repaired
The painter who coats the frames they weld
A contractor who hires the shop for site work

questions.stem: The welders keep passing frames to the painting bay with spatter and sharp edges still on them. Who suffers in the end?
options: Only the painter, who has extra grinding to do
The client, through delays and a poorer finish
Nobody, because paint covers spatter well
Only the welders, who must work more slowly

questions.stem: A client in Mandeville asks for 'a strong gate'. Which question helps most to pin down what she needs?
options: How wide is the opening, and will cars drive through?
Do you want it done fast or done right?
Have you asked any other shops for a price?
Would you like us to choose the colour?

questions.stem: Why should the team leader measure a window opening on site before burglar bars are made, rather than use the client's own figures?
options: Clients are not allowed to measure their homes
Measuring on site lets the shop charge a much higher price
The client's tape is sure to be the wrong type
Errors in size mean remaking, delay and extra cost

questions.stem: A client asks why hot-dip galvanised railings cost more than painted mild steel ones. What is the best explanation?
options: Galvanising makes the steel much stronger
It is only fashion, as good paint lasts just as long as zinc
Galvanised steel needs no welding at all
The zinc coat protects the steel from rust for much longer

questions.stem: Your shop sends gates out to be galvanised, which takes about a week. Why should that week be built into the finish date you give the client?
options: So you give a finish date that you can meet
So the client pays the galvaniser directly
So the client can collect the gate from the galvaniser
So the job looks bigger than it really is

questions.stem: A farmer brings an empty fuel drum and asks you to cut the top off with a torch, now, while he waits. What should you do?
options: Cut it at once, as an empty drum cannot burn
Refuse until it is cleaned and proved gas free
Cut it outside in the yard, where any fumes can blow away
Fill it with air from the compressor first

questions.stem: A client wants burglar bars welded shut over every bedroom window of her house. What is the best advice?
options: Fit them exactly as asked, since the client is paying for it
Refuse the job, as burglar bars are unlawful
Advise an opening grille so people can escape a fire
Fit them, but make the bars thinner

questions.stem: A client asks you to weld a crack in her household LPG cylinder. What should you do?
options: Refuse, and tell her to return it to the gas supplier
Weld it if it is empty and the valve is closed
Weld it with a low current and a small rod
Fill it with water, weld it, then test it with soap at home

questions.stem: Your shop promises every client a written quotation within two working days of a site visit. What is this kind of promise called?
options: A guarantee of quality
A variation
A purchase order
A service standard

questions.stem: Three months after a gate was fitted near the sea at Ocho Rios, the client complains of rust spots at the welds. What should the team leader do first?
options: Tell her rust near the sea is not your problem
Listen, apologise, and arrange to inspect it
Send a painter at once without looking at it
Offer a discount on her next order instead

questions.stem: The rust turns out to be because welds were painted without the slag and spatter being cleaned off. What should follow the repair?
options: Nothing more is needed, as the client is now happy
Blame the painting bay for it, in front of the client
Change the shop's finishing checks so it does not recur
Stop offering painted gates to any clients

questions.stem: A client rings the workshop to say her grille was invoiced twice. Only the office handles invoices. What should the welding team leader do?
options: Tell her it is not his department
Promise her a refund himself on the spot
Ask her to stop phoning the workshop about money matters
Pass it to the office and tell her who will call

questions.stem: While a hotel's maintenance manager describes a broken kitchen trolley, how do you show that you have understood?
options: Sum up the fault and what he needs, then check
Start the repair before he finishes speaking
Nod and look at your phone while he talks
Tell him about a harder job you did last week

questions.stem: A restaurant in Negril wants a new steel worktable for its kitchen. Which material should you advise?
options: Painted mild steel, as it is cheapest
Galvanised steel, as it never rusts
Food-grade stainless steel
Aluminium painted with enamel

questions.stem: When handing over a new sliding gate, what should the team show the client?
options: How to weld the track if it ever breaks
How to use, lock and look after the gate
How to remove the stops and the guides
How to repaint it in a different colour

questions.stem: Why should the shop keep the drawings of a client's security grilles and strong-room door private?
options: Others could use them to break in
The drawings are protected by GCT law
So other shops cannot copy the price
So the client must come back for repairs

questions.stem: Which job record best helps the shop if the same client calls back about a trailer hitch you repaired?
options: The welder's name and the time he spent on it
The price charged, and the date it was paid
A photo of the trailer, with no notes on it
Date, fault found, work done, parts used and welder

questions.stem: The fitter needs the cutting list for a staircase before he can start. How does the team leader serve him best?
options: Tell him the sizes from memory as needed
Give him a clear, checked list on time
Let him measure from the drawing himself
Send it after the welders have started

questions.stem: The shop's inspector rejects a frame because the welds are oversize. What is the best response from the welding team?
options: Argue that bigger welds are always stronger
Ignore it, since the client will not notice
Ask what the drawing needs and put it right
Send the frame out before he checks again

questions.stem: A client asks you to sign a paper saying the trailer you worked on was 'inspected and certified'. You only welded on one bracket. What should you do?
options: Decline, and state only the work you did
Sign it, since the trailer looks safe enough
Sign it if he pays an extra fee for it
Ask the apprentice to sign it instead

questions.stem: An elderly client finds it hard to read the small print on your quotation. How should you help?
options: Tell him to ask a grandchild to read it
Send the same quotation again by email
Leave it, since he can sign without reading
Go through it with him and give large print

questions.stem: Why should the team leave a client's yard swept, with offcuts and rod stubs removed, after site welding?
options: It is only needed if the client asks for it
So the next shop cannot see your methods
It shows care, and stubs can burn or cut people
It is not needed, as clients clean their own yards

questions.stem: A client's staircase will be four days late because the steel arrived late. When should you tell the client?
options: On the day it was due, if he asks
As soon as you know, with a new date
Only after it is finished and fitted
Never; small delays are normal

questions.stem: Halfway through making a set of balcony rails, the client asks for a different pattern of bars. What is the best response?
options: Agree the added cost and time in writing first
Change the pattern at once to keep him happy
Refuse, as the design has already started
Make the change but bill him without telling him

questions.stem: The shop gives a 6-month warranty on its workmanship. A hinge weld on a gate cracks after 4 months of normal use. What should the shop do?
options: Charge for the repair, as it is now old work
Repair it free and find out why it cracked
Tell the client hinges are not covered
Ask the client to weld it himself

questions.stem: A client is angry and raising his voice in the shop office about a delayed water tank. What is the best first step?
options: Raise your voice to match his
Walk away until he calms down
Tell him the delay is his own fault
Stay calm, listen fully and let him finish

questions.stem: A client reads 'prices exclude GCT' on your quotation and asks what it means. What do you tell her?
options: GCT will not be charged on this job
GCT is already in the price shown
GCT is added on top, at the current rate
GCT is paid only by the shop

questions.stem: Before work starts on a J$140 000 security door, the shop asks for 30% of the price. How much must the client pay before work starts?
Of 60 clients surveyed, 48 said they would use the shop again. What percentage is that?
The delivery driver needs the size and mass of a steel tank before he collects it. Why should the team leader give him this in writing?
options: So he can charge the client for fuel
So the client can see the tank's full price on the note
So he brings the right truck and lifting gear
So he can leave the tank at any site

questions.stem: Your team must weld a new security door on a busy shop in Half Way Tree during opening hours. What should you agree with the owner first?
options: Nothing, as the work only takes a day
Times, barriers and where sparks and fumes will go
That his staff will hold the door while you weld it on
That he pays in cash before you start

questions.stem: While your team welds at a client's house, her children come to watch the arc. What should you do?
options: Stop, and keep them back behind a screen
Let them watch, as it is good for them to learn
Give them old sunglasses to watch through
Carry on, as the arc is only harmful up close

questions.stem: The shop's records show that 1 in 5 jobs needs a return visit to fix something. What does this suggest?
options: Clients are too fussy about small things
Return visits are a good way to meet clients
The welders should work faster on each job
Quality checks before handover need improving

questions.stem: A client cannot understand why a small trailer repair needs a full day. What is the best way to explain?
options: Tell him that welding is too hard to explain
Give him the price and tell him to take it or leave it
Walk him through the steps: strip, weld, test, paint
Say the shop is busy and he must wait his turn

questions.stem: The stores clerk asks welders to sign for every packet of electrodes they draw. Why should the team leader support this?
options: It slows the welders down on purpose
It shows where stock goes, so it can be reordered
It lets the clerk charge the welders for each rod used
It is only needed when an auditor visits

questions.stem: A week after a complaint about a sagging gate was put right, what should the team leader do?
options: Nothing, as the matter is now closed
Send the client a bill for the visit
Ask her to post a good review online
Call to check she is happy with the repair

questions.stem: A client wants the cheapest possible frame for a stand that will hold a full water tank. What should you do?
options: Explain the load and safe sizes, then quote
Use the thinnest steel he asks for
Refuse the job without explaining why
Make it cheaply from scrap steel lying in the yard

questions.stem: Your team keeps missing the collection times promised to clients. Which step would help most?
options: Stop giving clients any collection dates at all from now
Plan jobs on a board and check progress daily
Promise later dates and finish early
Blame the supplier for every late job

questions.stem: A site carpenter says your team's steel base plate is blocking his formwork and asks you to shift it. How should you respond?
options: Move it at once, as he asked
Refuse, because masons cannot tell welders what to do
Check the drawing and agree it with the site lead
Tell him to move it himself

questions.stem: Over the weekend, a welder borrows the shop's engine-driven welder to do private jobs for the shop's own clients. Why is this a problem?
options: It takes the shop's work and uses its equipment
It is fine as long as he puts fuel back in the machine
It is fine if the clients are happy
It is only a problem if the machine breaks

questions.stem: When a client collects a fabricated tank, which documents should she receive?
options: Only a receipt for the cash paid
The shop's full price list and a business card
A copy of the welder's pay slip
The invoice, any test results and care notes

questions.stem: A service standard says quotations go out within 48 hours of the site visit. The visit was on Monday at 2 p.m. What is the latest the quotation may go out?
options: Tuesday at 2 p.m.
Wednesday at 2 p.m.
Thursday at 2 p.m.
Wednesday at 9 a.m.

questions.stem: A client who uses a wheelchair orders a new gate for her home. Which question should you ask her?
options: Whether someone else in the house will sign the order for her
Whether she wants the cheapest gate
How she wants to open and lock it from her chair
Whether she needs the gate at all

questions.stem: Why should a shop call a client a few days after fitting a large gate?
options: To check it works well and fix any snags early
To ask for more money for extra hours
To try to sell her a second gate in the same week
To find out where she bought the paint

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: The painting bay cannot start until the welders pass on finished frames. In customer service terms, what is the painting bay to the welders?
A hotel that buys steel railings from the shop is what kind of customer?
A client pays a J$30 000 deposit on a J$120 000 job. What percentage of the price is the deposit?
Which word names the shop's promise, given in writing with the invoice, to repair its own faulty welding free for a stated period?
A gate is quoted at J$96 000 before GCT. The client pays half now. How much is paid now, before GCT, in J$?
A client is told her railings will be 'HDG'. Which finish, done in a bath of melted zinc, do these letters stand for?
A client was promised her grille in 10 working days, but it was ready on day 13. By what percentage did the shop overrun its promise?
Of 50 gates delivered this quarter, 45 were ready by the promised date. What percentage were on time?
Which document, signed by the client when goods are handed over, proves that the shop delivered them?
What is the name for the card or sheet that travels with a job through the shop, listing the work, materials and checks?
A gate needs 3 working days to make, 5 working days at the galvaniser and 1 day to fit. What is the least lead time, in working days, to give the client?
What is the name for the shop function that checks welded work against the drawing and standard before it goes to the client?
Which metal is chosen for food-contact surfaces, such as kitchen worktables, because it resists rust and is easy to keep clean?
What is the part payment a client makes before work starts, to secure the order and pay for materials?
Steel near the coast rusts faster because of salt in the air. What one word describes this kind of setting, as in a '______ environment'?

essays.stem: Name the internal customers and the external customers of a fabrication shop's welding team. For two of each, explain what they need from the team and how the team can serve them well.
essays.modelAnswer: Internal customers are people inside the business who depend on the welding team's work: the fitters, the painting bay, the inspector, the stores, the office and the delivery driver. External customers are the people and firms who buy from the shop: home owners, hotels, farmers, factories and contractors. The painting bay needs frames on time, with slag, spatter and sharp edges removed, so the team should clean and check each frame before passing it on. The office needs accurate hours and materials for each job, so it can invoice on time; the team leader should hand in the sheets every Friday. A home owner ordering a gate needs the right size, a good finish and the date kept, so the team should measure on site and keep her informed. A contractor needs the work to fit the programme and the drawings, so the team should check revisions and agree delivery times. Good internal service makes good external service possible.
markingPoints: Defines internal customers with welding-shop examples
Defines external customers with examples
Two internal customers: their needs and how to serve them
Two external customers: their needs and how to serve them
Links internal service to the service the client receives

essays.stem: A hotel in Montego Bay asks your shop to make and fit new steel railings around its pool deck. Describe how you would find out and confirm exactly what the client needs before you quote.
essays.modelAnswer: I would arrange a site visit with the hotel's maintenance manager and ask open questions: what the railings are for, who uses the area, the style they want, any height or safety rules they must meet, the budget and the date the area must reopen. I would measure every run, the height and the fixing surface myself and take photos. Because the pool is near the sea and uses chlorine, I would explain the choice of material: stainless steel or hot-dip galvanised and painted steel last far longer than painted mild steel. I would ask about working hours, so guests are not disturbed by noise and sparks. Back at the shop I would make a sketch with sizes and send it with my notes, asking the manager to confirm. Only when the needs are agreed in writing would I prepare the quotation, listing what is and is not included.
markingPoints: Site visit with open questions on use, style, rules, budget and dates
Measures and photographs the site personally
Advises on material for a coastal, chlorinated setting
Plans around the hotel's guests and working hours
Sends a sketch and notes for written confirmation before quoting

essays.stem: A client brings an old fuel drum and asks you to cut it in half with a torch so he can make a barbecue. Explain how you would handle the request so that he stays safe and still feels well served.
essays.modelAnswer: I would thank him and explain calmly that I cannot cut the drum with a torch as it is. A drum that held fuel can still contain vapour even when it looks empty, and heat or sparks can make it explode, which has killed welders. I would not just say no; I would offer safe choices. The drum could be cleaned thoroughly and tested by a competent person as gas free before any hot work, following the shop's hot work procedure, or we could cut it with a cold method after cleaning, or build the barbecue from new steel sheet. I would give him the price and time for each choice so he can decide. If he insists on a quick torch cut, I would politely refuse and record the request. By explaining the danger in plain words and offering another way, I keep everyone safe and he still leaves with a solution.
markingPoints: Explains the danger of vapour in an 'empty' fuel drum in plain words
Does not do hot work on it as it is
Offers safe options: cleaning and gas-free test, cold cutting, or new steel
Gives price and time so the client can choose
Stays polite, refuses firmly if pressed, and records it

essays.stem: A client complains that the gate your shop fitted three months ago has rust spots and now drags on the ground. Describe how you would deal with the complaint from the first call to the follow-up, and how you would stop it happening again.
essays.modelAnswer: On the first call I would listen without interrupting, apologise for the trouble, take her details and record the complaint. I would agree a time to visit soon. On site I would inspect the gate with her: check where the rust is, whether the welds were cleaned before painting, and why it drags, for example a worn hinge, a weak hinge weld or a post that has moved. I would explain what I found in plain words and agree the repair and the date. Because the work is under warranty, there would be no charge if the fault is ours. After the repair I would check that the gate swings freely and ask her to confirm she is happy. A few days later I would call to follow up. Back at the shop I would find the root cause and change our method, for example adding a cleaning and inspection check before painting, and a hinge check at handover.
markingPoints: Listens, apologises and records the complaint
Visits quickly and inspects with the client to find the cause
Explains the findings and agrees the repair, applying the warranty fairly
Checks the repair with the client and follows up later
Finds the root cause and changes the shop's checks

essays.stem: Explain to a client, in plain words, the difference between painted mild steel, hot-dip galvanised steel and stainless steel for outdoor railings near the sea, and how you would help her choose.
essays.modelAnswer: I would say: painted mild steel is the cheapest at first. The paint keeps air and salt away from the steel, but near the sea it chips and the steel under it starts to rust, so it needs repainting often. Hot-dip galvanised steel is dipped in hot zinc, which coats every surface, inside and out. The zinc protects the steel even where it is scratched, so it lasts much longer; it can also be painted for colour. Stainless steel does not need a coating and stays bright with little care, but it costs the most, and it needs the right grade and regular washing near salt water. To help her choose, I would ask how long she wants the railings to last, how much upkeep she is willing to do, the look she wants and her budget. I would give a price for each choice and the likely upkeep, then let her decide.
markingPoints: Painted mild steel: cheapest, but rusts and needs repainting near the sea
Galvanised: zinc coat protects even at scratches; lasts longer; can be painted
Stainless: little upkeep, highest cost, right grade and washing needed
Uses plain words a client understands
Helps her choose by asking about life, upkeep, look and budget, with prices

essays.stem: As welding team leader, explain what the stores, the painting bay, the inspector and the office each need from your team, and what you would change so that each is served better.
essays.modelAnswer: For the stores, the team leader can make sure requests are written clearly with size, type and quantity, given early enough, and that welders sign for what they draw and return unused rods and offcuts. For the painting bay, frames should be passed on clean, free of slag, spatter and sharp edges, labelled with the job number and at the agreed time, so painting is not held up. For the inspector, the team should check its own work against the drawing first, mark each item clearly, keep the WPS and records with the job, and accept findings without argument, putting faults right quickly. For the office, hours and materials sheets should be accurate and handed in on time so invoices go out, and any changes the client asked for should be reported at once. The team leader can agree these points with each group, review them at a short weekly meeting and fix any problems.
markingPoints: Stores: clear, early requests; signing for and returning stock
Painting bay: clean, labelled frames on time
Inspector: self-check, records with the job, accept and fix findings
Office: accurate, on-time sheets; changes reported
Agrees standards with each group and reviews them regularly

essays.stem: Explain how a fabrication shop can set service standards for its clients, such as for quotations, collection dates and returned calls, and how it can measure and use the results.
essays.modelAnswer: A service standard is a clear, measurable promise. The shop could set: every message returned the same working day; a written quotation within two working days of a site visit; at least nine out of ten jobs ready by the promised date; and every complaint answered within one day. The standards should be agreed with the team so they are realistic, written down and shown to staff. To measure them, the office keeps a simple log of messages, quotation dates, promised and actual collection dates, and complaints. Each month the team leader works out the results, for example 45 of 50 jobs on time is 90%. Where the shop falls short, the team looks for the cause, such as late steel or poor planning, and fixes it. Good results can be shared with the team and used in the shop's advertising. Standards should be reviewed each year and raised as the shop improves.
markingPoints: Explains a service standard as a clear, measurable promise
Gives realistic examples for quotes, dates, calls and complaints
Keeps simple records to measure each standard
Works out results and acts on shortfalls by finding causes
Shares results and reviews or raises the standards

essays.stem: A steel staircase your team made has just been fixed in a client's house in Kingston. Describe the handover: what you would check first, what you would show and explain to the client, and what papers you would leave.
essays.modelAnswer: Before handover I would check the work against the drawing and our snag list, and make sure the site is clean, with offcuts and rod stubs removed. With the client I would walk round the item and show what was done, pointing out any changes agreed during the job. For a staircase I would show the handrail fixings and explain the safe load if one was given by the designer. For a tank stand I would explain the load it was designed for and that it must not be overloaded or have extra tanks added without advice. I would explain care: wash salt and dust off, check the paint once a year and touch up chips quickly, and do not weld or cut anything on it later without advice. I would hand over the invoice, the warranty terms, any test or inspection records, the care notes and our contact details, and ask the client to sign the delivery note.
markingPoints: Checks the work and the site before handover
Walks through the work with the client, noting changes
Explains safe use and limits (loads, no added items without advice)
Explains care and maintenance
Hands over invoice, warranty, records and care notes; gets a signature

essays.stem: One walk-in client is more at ease speaking Jamaican Creole and is unsure about written quotations; another is a visitor who speaks mainly Spanish. Explain how you would serve each fairly and make sure both understand what they are agreeing to.
essays.modelAnswer: Both clients deserve the same respect, time and honest prices. With the first client, I would speak in the way he is comfortable with and never talk down to him. I would go through the quotation line by line in plain words, show a sketch of the item, point to the price, the deposit, what is included and the finish date, and ask him to tell me back what he understands. I would offer to read anything he wants read and give him time to think before signing. With the visitor, I would use simple English, sketches, numbers written down and photos of similar work. If a colleague or someone he trusts speaks Spanish, I would ask them to help, or use a phone translation tool for key points, then check understanding with simple questions. For both, I would confirm everything in writing, keep a copy, and make sure the price and terms are the same as any other client would get.
markingPoints: Treats both with equal respect, time and fair prices
Uses plain words, sketches and line-by-line explanation for the first client
Uses simple English, visuals and a helper or translation for the visitor
Checks understanding by asking them to explain back
Confirms everything in writing and keeps a copy

essays.stem: Your shop promised a client her burglar bars by Friday, but the steel delivery has been delayed. Explain what you would do and why keeping the client informed matters.
essays.modelAnswer: As soon as I knew about the delay, I would find out the real new delivery date from the supplier, and check whether another supplier could supply the same steel sooner at a fair price. I would re-plan the job: perhaps prepare the fixings, templates and paint so that the bars can be made quickly once the steel arrives. Then, well before Friday, I would call the client, apologise, explain the reason honestly and give her a new date I am sure we can keep. If her home is not secure meanwhile, I would ask whether a temporary measure would help. I would confirm the new date in writing and update her if anything changes. Keeping her informed matters because it shows respect, lets her plan, and keeps her trust. A client who hears bad news early is usually understanding; one who finds out on the day feels let down and may not return or may tell others.
markingPoints: Finds the real new date and looks for another source
Re-plans the work to save time later
Calls the client before the due date, apologises and explains honestly
Gives a realistic new date and confirms it in writing
Explains why: trust, respect, lets her plan, protects the shop's name

practical1.title: Role play: site visit, measured sketch and written quotation for a fabricated gate
practical1.brief: Your group is the sales and estimating team of a fabrication shop. The assessor plays a client who wants a new vehicle gate (or gives a client card to one member to play the part), and marks out a 'gateway' at the Centre. Share the roles: one member leads the client interview, one measures the opening and takes photos, one draws a measured sketch of the gate, one works out the steel, consumables and hours with the prices the assessor gives, and one writes the quotation and confirms it with the client. Every member must speak to the client at least once and sign the part of the paperwork they prepared. The quotation must show the work, the material and finish (with your advice on why), what is not included, the price in J$, GCT 'at the current rate', the deposit, the time to finish (allowing for galvanising if chosen) and the warranty. End by explaining the quotation to the client and recording any changes. Photograph each stage.
materials: Client card or brief from the assessor, and a marked-out 'gateway' at the Centre
Measuring tape (5 m or longer), spirit level and camera or phone
Squared paper, pencils, rulers and a calculator
Price list for steel, consumables, galvanising and labour (from the assessor, made-up figures)
Client needs record and quotation templates
photos: The client interview, with the needs record being filled in
The opening being measured, with the tape on the posts
The measured sketch of the gate, with sizes
The finished quotation, signed by the members who prepared it
The quotation being explained to the client
checklist: Asked open questions and recorded the client's needs fully (use, size, style, security, budget, date)
Measured accurately and recorded the sizes and site conditions
Advised on material and finish in plain words, with reasons
Worked out quantities and costs correctly, with GCT shown as 'at the current rate'
Wrote a clear quotation stating what is and is not included, the deposit, the time and the warranty
Explained the quotation politely and checked the client understood
Spoke to the client at least once and signed their own part
safety: Keep the role-play area clear of trip hazards and moving equipment
If measuring near the workshop, wear safety boots and stay out of marked welding areas
Treat the client's details as confidential and do not take them away from the Centre
Speak respectfully at all times, even when the client is difficult

practical2.title: Handle a complaint about a finished frame, inspect it and agree internal service standards
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a welded frame or gate section 'returned by a client', with faults planted in it (for example rust at uncleaned welds, sharp edges, a size outside tolerance, a cracked or missing weld), and a complaint card. Part 1: two members role play the complaint call, one as the client and one as the team leader, while another records the complaint on the complaint log. Part 2: the whole group inspects the frame against the drawing: each member checks and marks one kind of fault (size, welds, finish, edges), measures and photographs it, and writes it on an inspection sheet. Part 3: the group writes the reply to the client (what was found, the repair offered and the date) and a root-cause note. Part 4: the group writes a one-page 'internal service agreement' between welding, stores, the painting bay and the inspector to stop the faults recurring, and presents it as a poster. Every member signs the part they wrote.
materials: Welded frame or gate section with planted faults, its drawing and a complaint card (from the assessor)
Measuring tape, steel rule, square and a fillet weld gauge
Chalk or paint marker for marking faults
Complaint log, inspection sheet and reply templates
Flip-chart paper and markers for the poster
Leather gloves and safety glasses for handling the frame
photos: The complaint role play, with the complaint log being filled in
Each fault marked on the frame and measured
The written reply to the client and the root-cause note
checklist: Listened, apologised and recorded the complaint accurately and politely
Inspected the frame against the drawing and found the planted faults
Measured and recorded each fault clearly, with photos
Wrote a reply that explains the findings and offers a fair repair and date
Identified a likely root cause for each fault
Helped write clear, measurable internal service standards
Signed their own part and took part in the presentation
safety: Wear gloves when handling the frame; it may have sharp edges and burrs
Lift the frame with two people or a lifting aid, and support it on trestles
Keep the role play respectful; no shouting or personal remarks
